utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-65/1-S, the Prosecutor versus Predrag Banovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And appearances?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Please, Your Honours. I appear for the Prosecution. My name is Sureta Chana. And I am assisted by Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my name is Jovan Babic. I'm an attorney from Serbia and Montenegro. And today I appear for the accused, Predrag Banovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The accused Predrag Banovic entered into a plea agreement with the Prosecutor and pleaded guilty to count 1 of the indictment at a hearing on June 26th. At that hearing, the Chamber accepted the plea and entered a finding of guilt. The purpose of this hearing therefore is to determine a sentence. We begin with the Prosecutor, but I remind you that we have your briefs, and your submissions need not be unduly long. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, the Prosecutor considers it its duty to bring to the Court's attention certain issues which have been raised by the Defence in their sentencing brief. Although as Your Honour stated the accused pleaded guilty and conviction has been entered, there are some assertions in the sentencing brief which may tend to suggest that the plea was not an informed one or indeed it was not unequivocal. To that end, Your Honours, we would like to bring the Court's attention to the contents of paragraph 33 and paragraphs 46. To the extent that the assertions made therein can be considered to be inconsistent with the guilty plea or an informed plea of guilty. The question, therefore, is now whether the comments now being made may indicate that the guilty plea was somehow not valid at the time it was made. The Prosecution stands guided by the Court in that regard. If I may read out the two paragraphs to which I'm alluding, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's deal first with 33.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 33, Your Honours, inter alia says, and that is the second half of the paragraph, I'll read from there: "Although he's of the opinion that he did not kill anyone while beating him, he admitted that he had reason to believe that the injuries that the participants in the crime inflicted to prisoners resulted in death of a victim, so he admitted that he was capable of committing a crime." Your Honours, I now turn to paragraph 46. Again, I read from the second half of the paragraph. The accused did not find a way to resist the power of his superiors nor the force of those who wilfully barged into the camp, committed crimes, and forced him and others to commit crimes, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what is the interpretation that you put on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused appears to be raising the defence of duress. While we appreciate that duress is not a defence for wilfully taking life, but it could be a defence for the beating charges. And in the accused, having raised that defence of duress, or it tends to that suggest that he is raising such a defence would compromise the plea to some extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're familiar with the Erdemovic decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. It's the very same issue that arose in that, amongst others, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The essence of that decision, as I understand it, is that duress is not a complete defence, but that it may be a relevant factor in mitigation of sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, it may be a relevant factor in mitigating in taking life, but whether it's a mitigating factor alone in respect of the beatings is still subject to an appellate decision, Your Honour, which I believe we have still not got a definitive stand on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What decision that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Erdemovic decision, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying that Erdemovic was not definitive as to the question of beating?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, the Erdemovic decision was very much confined to a soldier, and superior orders. And they said while it could be a defence for a soldier to take -- that he could not take him alive, it may not be to the extent of beating that duress would not be a -- could be a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I myself don't see why it would be significantly different, why the law would be significantly different in relation to a civilian. But do you have any more submissions on that before we go to paragraph 33?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No. In respect of paragraph 46, Your Honours, those would be my submissions. And of course the Prosecution stands always guided by the Court, but this is just to alert the Court that it satisfies itself that the plea, in fact, is a proper one. We ourselves consider it to be so, and subject to confirmation of Mr. Babic that it is, and his client has been apprised that in fact -- it is a properly entered plea, we are prepared to proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that you are satisfied that the plea is a proper one, notwithstanding what you see as some ambiguity in paragraph 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is ambiguity, and it is our duty to bring it to the attention of the Court. A plea must be unqualified and reserved unequivocal and informed. If there's anything which tends to suggest that it was neither one of these elements, then the Court has to satisfy itself, Your Honours, that it is properly entered. It is simply our duty to bring it to the attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I think you're quite correct in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we look at 33 now. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Your Honour, I'm just getting to the page. Again, this somehow qualifies his guilty plea, Your Honour, when he says, or does not make it unequivocal, that he's of the opinion he did not kill anyone, although he has accepted responsibility in his guilty plea of having murdered or participating in the beating of five victims who died as a result of those beatings. But he then says he's capable of committing a crime. Your Honour, once again, we simply bring this to the Court's attention. And if the Court still finds that it is a proper plea -- I mean, it is -- the plea was taken after an agreement which had been entered into by the Prosecution and the Defence. The factual basis was agreed upon. We are informed by Mr. Babic that he fully apprised his client of the consequences of this plea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before I ask Mr. Babic to respond, just go back to paragraph 46, which I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Is a more substantial issue --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Than 33. The heading of that -- of those paragraphs is the lowest rank and subordinated position in the police authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it not the case that what is being done here is to suggest that by virtue of the low rank of the accused, and I believe at another place, there is also a reference to his low intelligence --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- That he was somehow subject or susceptible to influence, and that this is something which the accused would want us to consider in sentence. But let me ask Mr. Babic to comment, first on 46. And you were the counsel in Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Due to circumstances, Your Honour, I was counsel in the Erdemovic case for the Defence, and I do have experience which is valid in this case. In no way did the Defence intend, nor does it wish to bring into question the plea agreement made between the accused and the Prosecution. The titles, in our submission, suggest quite clearly the interpretation I wish to place upon each fact and each circumstances. Never did we say that this could be either a partial or complete defence, but simply a mitigating circumstance that we suggest the Chamber consider. The same applies to paragraphs 33 and 46. I put the accused Banovic within the context of the Keraterm camp bearing in view his youth, his psychological maturity, and the impossibility for him to discern, to tell what is good and what is bad, and the way he acted. It is quite clear that what we are asking is that the Chamber take this as a mitigating circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. The Chamber, having heard submissions from the Prosecutor for which the Chamber is grateful, and from Mr. Babic concludes that the plea is informed and is not equivocal. So thank you, Ms. Chana. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will now with Your Honours permission proceed with the sentencing arguments. Predrag Banovic has been convicted following a plea of guilty of one count of persecution. The Trial Chamber has before it the plea agreement dated 21st June, 2003, which contains a statement which contains the factual basis of the crime of which Predrag Banovic has been convicted. I do not propose to repeat all those facts today, Your Honours. But in brief, Predrag Banovic performed duties as a guard at the Keraterm camp. Keraterm camp was one of the three major camps established by the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff in the municipality of Prijedor. The camp began operating on 23rd May, 1992, and held as many as 1.500 detainees. Persons detained in the Keraterm camp between the end of May to the time when the camp closed in mid-August 1992 were primarily Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croat males of military age, whilst all the guards were Serbs. These camps operated in a manner designed to ill-treat and persecute non-Serbs from Prijedor and other areas with the sole aim of ridding the territory of non-Serbs or of subjugating those who remained. Detention of non-Serbs in the camps was a prelude to killing them or transferring them to non-Serb areas. Conditions at the camp were brutal, inhumane, and degrading, and resulted in the physical debilitation or death of the detainees. Detainees were regularly subjected to severe beatings, killings, and other forms of physical and psychological mistreatment by camp authorities, as well as the so-called visitors to the camp. The single count of persecution of which Predrag Banovic has been convicted has three components, Your Honour. First, it encompasses Banovic's participation in five murders, the victims being detainees in the camp, who succumbed to beatings in which Predrag Banovic participated. Secondly, it encompasses the beatings of 22 other detainees at Keraterm camp in which Predrag Banovic participated. Thirdly, it encompasses inhumane conditions, including humiliation, harassment, and psychological abuse suffered by non-Serbs at Keraterm camp during the course of their confinement therein. Your Honours, the sentencing brief filed by the Prosecution on 17 July puts forward the Prosecution's arguments and position as to sentence in line with the plea agreement and factual basis as agreed by the Prosecution and the Defence. The Prosecution recommends to the Trial Chamber that it impose a sentence of eight years. Your Honours, both the Prosecution and the Defence acknowledge that the Trial Chamber is not bound by the sentence recommended by the Prosecution. Nevertheless, it can form the basis of your deliberations. The Prosecution submits that is the appropriate sentence in all the circumstances of this particular case. Before addressing the sentencing factors specifics to this case, I would make a number of general submissions. First, I would submit that there's always an overriding consideration that sentencing must promote the purposes of the criminal law. International law, like national legal systems, criminalises certain conduct for the protection of common human values and a commitment to the accepted norms of civilised behaviour shared and upheld by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. international community. Sentencing promotes that purpose by deterring violations of the criminal law. In the Celebici appeal judgement at paragraph 799 to 803, the Appeals Chamber has accepted the general importance of deterrence as a consideration in sentencing for international crimes, subject, of course, to a proviso that this factor must not be accorded undue prominence. Secondly, the Appeals Chamber has held that retribution is an important factor in sentencing. In the Aleksovski appeal judgement at paragraph 185, the Appeals Chamber explained that the concept of retribution, and I quote: "It is not to be understood as fulfilling a desire for revenge, but as duly expressing the outrage of the international community of these crimes. Accordingly, a sentence of the International Tribunal should make plain the condemnation of the international community of the behaviour in question and show that the international community was not ready to tolerate serious violations of international humanitarian law and human rights." Your Honours, the Prosecution respectfully submits that this purpose of signalling the international community's condemnation would be undermined if sentences imposed by the Tribunal were lower than those generally imposed by national courts. This could send a message, for instance, that a killing of a person as a war crime or a crime against humanity or as a part of genocide is less serious and morally less reprehensible than an ordinary murder under national law. The true position is contrary, and this should be reflected in sentencing. My third general submission, Your Honours, relates to the fact that Predrag Banovic can be categorised as a low-level perpetrator, or the so-called "small fish." It is acknowledged that as a guard, Predrag Banovic did not hold any rank, and that when he was on duty, he had no control over other guards and did not himself have power to punish anybody. It is not contended that Predrag Banovic participated in the formulation of the criminal policy of the Bosnian Serb leadership or that he was responsible for the establishment of the Keraterm camp. Your Honours, the Defence in its sentencing brief asks this Trial Chamber to consider his low rank and subordinate position as a mitigating factor and relies, and I quote: "On the jurisprudence of this Tribunal for that assertion." With respect, we disagree. The Trial Chamber in the Jelisic trial judgement at paragraph 133 pointed out: "Although the crimes perpetrated during armed conflicts may be more specifically ascribed to one or other of the principal political or military officials, they could not achieve their ends out the enthusiastic help or contribution, direct or indirect, of small fish such as the accused in that case." On appeal in that case, the Appeals Chamber rejected a Defence argument that the Trial Chamber had erred in taking this into account. Your Honours, the establishment of the Keraterm camp was part of a joint criminal enterprise of great magnitude which required of necessity many participants and institutions for its successful accomplishment and each participant and institution from the highest to the lowest level of authority contributed to its success. The plan's success depended on the engagement of Serb judicial, military, and security forces at all levels. I refer in this respect to paragraph 3 of the agreed facts. The objective of joint criminal enterprise was the permanent removal by force or other means of non-Serb inhabitants from the territory of the planned Serbian state within Bosnia and Herzegovina. Predrag Banovic was an essential cog in the machinery of this large-scale plan. Without the willing participation of low-level perpetrators like Predrag Banovic who participated willingly in the horrific crimes, no plan of such magnitude as we have here would be possible to achieve. The Prosecution submits that sentencing must reflect the fact that even the lowest level perpetrators are essential to the commission of large-scale crimes, and they cannot escape legal or moral culpability by pleading that they were only one of many who were caught up in events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Predrag Banovic knew of the system of ill treatment in the Keraterm camp. He intended to further this common concerted system of ill treatment. With that intention he committed the crimes of which he has been now convicted. The commission of these crimes by him contributed significantly to the joint criminal enterprise established at the camp. All of this, Your Honours, is reflected in paragraph 6 of the agreed facts. Your Honours, there can be no valid suggestion that he was acting under any form of duress or otherwise than as a completely willing participant. The sentence must reflect the fact that he was a knowing and significant contributor to extremely serious crimes. The sentence should equally make plain the condemnation of the international community of such behaviour of small fish and make it clear to any potential future perpetrator that such crimes will not pass unnoticed in the confusion of armed conflict and will not be ignored by the international community as a mere de minimus contribution to the large-scale destructive consequences of the armed conflict as a whole. I turn now to the sentencing factors specific to this case. These are dealt with in the Prosecution sentencing brief, and I merely refer to these. The crime in this case, which includes participation in five murders and the beating of 27 other victims, are inherently very grave. Murder in any legal system is one of the most serious crimes that a person can commit. As to the beatings, these were not mere assaults; rather, these beatings contributed in the large part to the atmosphere of terror in Keraterm camp and caused both serious physical and mental harm to the victims and mental harm to those who witnessed such events. Keraterm camp, Your Honours, has been referred to as a collection centre or a camp. It is of no relevance what term is used to describe it. However described, it was brutal and dehumanising for all the prisoners who were there. Powerless and vulnerable, at the mercy of the camp guards and the commanders which ran the camp with brutality. The Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, prisoners at the Keraterm camp, were kept in a state of constant physical and psychological terror. They were powerless and at the mercy of the guards and commanders. Your Honours, Predrag Banovic has admitted being a guard at the camp and in a position of authority over all the prisoners of the camp. He had the ability to make their life as comfortable as he could under the circumstances, or he could use his power over the prisoners to make their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already miserable existence even worse. Predrag Banovic chose to make it worse. The Rule 92 bis statements tendered by the Defence all state that Predrag Banovic had the ability to assist prisoners, and indeed provided selective help to some prisoners who had been his friends. Those statements equally reflect that he held himself out to them as a person who was in a position of sufficient authority to assist them in the event they were subjected to harassment by the authorities. These victims of Predrag Banovic are listed in the factual basis. It is important to read out their names in open court as an acknowledgment that ultimately these proceedings are about people who suffered at the Keraterm camp. Your Honours, I say this because the Prosecution received a call after Predrag Banovic pleaded guilty from a wife of a victim who perished at the Keraterm camp and who was extremely distressed that there was no acknowledgment of her husband's suffering and his death. With the Court's permission, I would like to read out their names in Court as a public acknowledgment of those victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise in advance for my pronunciation of the names, although I have tried. In the factual basis, paragraph 15, Your Honours, these five victims died as a result of the beatings inflicted upon them of which Predrag Banovic was a participant: Jovo Radocaj, Drago Tokmadzic, Jasmin Zvjezdas, Dzevad Karabegovic, Dzemal Mesic. Paragraph 16, Your Honours, are the victims and Predrag Banovic took part in the beatings of them. These are: Ramadan Bahonjic, Meho Kapetanovic, Faruk Hrncic, Enver Modronja, Adib Bajric, Uzeir Causevic aka Zejro, Saban Elezovic, Edin Ganic. The beating of three brothers Alisic: Armin, Edo, and a third brother whose first name is unknown. Ismet Garibovic, Vasif Mujkanovic, Mujo Sivac, Sulejman Sivac, Mirsad Karagic, Esad Islamovic. A prisoner with the name Mesic. Jasmin Ramadanovic, aka Sengin. Suad Halvadzic, and the beating of Besim Fazlic, Mehmed Avdic, Muharem Sivac, Mirsad Crljenkovic. A detainee called Smail. And lastly, the beating of Ismet Bajric. Predrag Banovic, Your Honours, by pleading guilty to his crimes and admitting his participation in the atmosphere of terror which prevailed at the Keraterm camp serves as a catharsis for victims and all people impacted by the war to start the healing process and to halt the cycle of personal or group retaliation in the area of conflict, thereby promoting reconciliation between the warring factions. While the Appeals Chamber noted that retribution is the only factor in punishment does not in itself bring justice and is inconsistent with the mandate of the Security Council, which is the restoration and the maintenance of peace in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, nevertheless the sentence ought to be proportionate to the crimes themselves. Your Honours, in the sentencing brief at paragraph 44 and 45 is the only expression of remorse which has been expressed by Predrag Banovic. The sentencing brief in those paragraphs suggests that the accused has shown remorse which was true and sincere in his interview to the investigators. Your Honours, since the interview has been filed under a seal of confidentiality, may I suggest that we go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Closed session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In conclusion, therefore, Your Honours, Predrag Banovic should be sentenced to neither more or less than he deserves, and there is absolutely no question that he deserves the eight years as recommended by the Prosecution. The very last point that I would add is that if anything the sentence should not be looked at as a precedent for other crimes of this nature, but the Prosecution does not recommend a higher sentence in this case. Unless there's anything else I can assist Your Honours on, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, was the eight years agreed at the time of plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me understand: How come you came to a conclusion on the same amount of time with such vast a difference in position?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm not -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not suggesting eight years is not too short a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I said exactly that he deserves the eight years that we have agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, the only matter that hasn't been dealt with, I think, in either brief is the issue of substantial cooperation. And I'm not seeking submissions. If it doesn't arise, it doesn't arise. But I just need to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's view is that there has not been substantial -- there has been some cooperation but by no means substantial cooperation. And unless Your Honours want -- it will involve me again going into private session if I want to discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I think I'd rather hear Mr. Babic first. If it's necessary, then you can come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, and my learned friends, in my submission, I set forth information that might be of assistance to the Trial Chamber in determining the sentence. I provided explanations and referred to the theory and also the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. At this public hearing, I wish to stress the main points in this submission and to provide some additional explanations. First of all, I wish to reiterate that the accused Banovic feels that the plea agreement he has concluded with the Prosecution is sacred and in no way does he wish to bring it into question. Secondly, the guilty plea entered by the accused before the beginning of the trial should undoubtedly be taken as a moral act contributing to the truth about the crimes in the Keraterm camp and his role in those crimes. Thirdly, the accused Banovic made this plea of his own free will. It was an informed plea, and he was fully aware of all the consequences of his plea. And fourthly, bearing in mind that sentencing is exclusively within the purview of this Trial Chamber, the Defence, relying on Rule 101(A), in its sentencing brief has put forward the relevant information that might assist the Trial Chamber in determining a sentence, supporting this information with 15 witness statements taken under Rule 92 bis, an expert report, and 9 exhibits. With your leave, Your Honours, the ninth exhibit, tab 9, is one to which I would add another document guaranteeing a job to the accused Banovic after he has served his sentence on the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is an addition, Mr. Babic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it's something that I received only yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the Prosecutor see it. It can be included in the bundle, and we'll consider its admission when we come to look at the admission of the documents as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. With all due respect, I'm convinced that you will accept the information contained in the brief, the witness statements and the exhibits, as they are elaborated in the brief. My starting point was that first of all, when determining a sentence, the purpose of punishment should be considered. Although this is not explicitly defined in the documents of this Tribunal, but the jurisprudence shows that the purposes are the protection of the international community, the achievement of peace and of reconciliation in the former Yugoslavia, retribution, deterrence, and rehabilitation of the accused. Under D, paragraph 20 to 58, and in the confidential addendum, I set out the factors that I feel this Trial Chamber should take into account when determining the sentence. I appeal to you, Your Honours, regarding the weight to be attached of each of these factors, that this should be in accordance with the goals I have mentioned. In connection with this, I wish to provide some additional explanations supporting the views I have put forward in paragraph 36 of my brief where I said that I believe that the gravity of the crime, and especially the role of the accused, should be put into the context of the aggressive wartime propaganda which was generally prevalent, but especially in Prijedor and in the Keraterm camp. The reason I mention this is that I am deeply convinced, based on my experience, and this is the third case I have been involved with before this Tribunal, that the role and influence of propaganda in the prewar period and during the war on the collective consciousness of each entity and each individual has not been given sufficient weight. I believe that the decisions of this Tribunal and of this particular Trial Chamber should provide an answer to question as to how a situation where in 1989, 80 per cent of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina responded in a questionnaire to the question of what the interethnic relations were, they said that they were good. How could this in the space of just a few years have been transformed into an atmosphere of hatred and crime and intolerance. I believe that this came about because of the rise of national parties and their propaganda relating to the threats against each of these entities and the need for their self-defense. I will summarise the propaganda on the Serbian side and link it up to the behaviour of the accused Banovic. So I will look into my own entity, and I hope that my learned friends in other cases defending Croats and Muslims will do the same. On the Serb side, the main propaganda line was put forward before this Trial Chamber by the accused Plavsic who said: "I am now convinced and I accept that several thousand innocent people were victims of the organised and systematic activity to remove Muslims and Croats from areas that the Serbs considered their own." To this she added that it was easy for her then to convince herself then that it was a question of survival and self-defense. Your Honours, if it was so easy for her to believe all of this, and she was an educated and experienced woman, then certainly it was far easier for a young, uneducated, inexperienced, and emotionally immature man such as the accused Banovic to believe this. The British journalist, Tim Jordan, wrote a book on the history, the myth, and the destruction of Yugoslavia where he said that the Serbs entered the war because their leaders took them to war. The leaders made use of the maligned threads in the history of their people to draw the people into Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. war. The issue of the survival and self-defense of the Serbian people was constantly raised by the media, including the media in Prijedor. Traumas were activated and abused. And as always in such situations, the spreading of rumours from individual to individual became a special form of propaganda. And the Keraterm camp is a very good example of this. On the one hand, the Serbs spread rumours about the crimes allegedly committed by some of the prisoners, and they used this as a reason to take revenge on them. On the other hand, the prisoners spread rumours on the crimes of the Banovic brothers, especially Predrag, while this Trial Chamber knows that only Predrag Banovic was in the camp and accepted the withdrawal of the indictment against Nenad. Also, during the discussions on agreed facts, and I wish to pay tribute to my learned friends in this respect, the murders of the Kuburas brothers and Fikret Abdic and some of the beatings were also withdrawn from this indictment. In an environment such as the Keraterm camp, there can be mistakes in identifying people. The essence of the rumours and the propaganda value of these rumours has been best expressed by the writer, Ivo Andric, a Nobel Prize winner who is deeply familiar with the mentality of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina who said in one of his books "the rumour started. Once a rumour starts, it doesn't stop. It continues, and it grows." The writer was writing about a prison. He was writing about the prisoners, the administration, and the prison guards. This is an environment that resembles the environment of the Keraterm camp. Your Honours, I wish to believe that when evaluating the witness statements of the Prosecution, you will bear in mind the quotation I have just mentioned and that you will place your trust in the agreed facts which form the factual basis of the guilty plea because this best expresses the role of the accused Predrag Banovic in the crimes committed in the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand your submission on this point: You're saying that the accused lived in an environment of propaganda such that he was influenced by it, he succumbed to the propaganda. And this is a factor that you're asking us to consider in determining sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now very briefly list the factors that the Chamber should take into consideration in sentencing. When discussing aggravating circumstances, I put forward my position that there are no aggravating circumstances in this case because they're essentially subsumed in the overall gravity of the offence. As for mitigating circumstances, in my view they are the following: First of all, the guilty plea, the remorse that the accused has expressed, and unlike the Office of the Prosecution, I believe that his remorse is sincere. Your Honours, the main problem in the interview between the accused Banovic and the investigators was that Predrag Banovic does not remember a single name. He does not know the names of the people who were in the camp. There are very few names that he was able to recall. That's why there was some confusion. But he did sign his guilty plea in the end. Secondly, his low rank and subservient position in the hierarchy. Then his personal circumstances, his youth. He was 22 at the time of the commission of the crimes. His family circumstances, he's married and the father of a three-year-old child. The fact that before the war, he lived and socialised with people of all ethnicities and religions, and that he did not have any discriminatory intent before the war but that it appeared during the war as a result of warmongering propaganda. During the war, he helped many Muslims and Croats in various ways. He has no prior criminal record. He was not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. During the war, he was an emotionally immature personality. His behaviour in the Detention Unit has been good. He has shown respect toward this Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. He's now fully aware of the social, moral, and legal context of his actions in the camp, and he is now ready to behave in a responsible and mature way. In other words, his character can be improved. I believe that he has cooperated significantly with the Prosecution, and I have given reasons for this view in my confidential addendum. Finally, the Defence feels that the guilty plea and the remorse shown, together with the factors I have already mentioned, should be given sufficient weight for the sentence to be an expression of justice which considers the suffering of the victims, but is also just for society as a whole, and the accused. In my view, an eight-year sentence would meet all these requirements. Thank you, Your Honours, and I will answer any questions you might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, perhaps you should say something about the substantial cooperation. If you need to do it in private session, then we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. May we go into closed or private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You wanted to add something, Mr. Babic? No. Yes, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, if you have no questions, I ask you to give the floor to the accused Banovic and allow him to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the accused, Mr. Banovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have pleaded unequivocally as guilty. My guilty plea was an expression of sincere remorse concerning the events in Prijedor, and especially the Keraterm camp. I gave an interview about my role in this to the investigators of the Tribunal. Today, I wish to add only the following: My arrest and transfer to The Hague, as well as that of my brother, was something I experienced with great fear, mostly because the propaganda was always that The Hague was a place for the quiet murder of the Serbs. Fortunately, very soon, I came to the conclusion that this propaganda was a lie. Through the proceedings up to this point, I have experienced enlightenment. I have gathered the strength to face the truth and myself. This is why I made the decision to change my plea. I deplore the period of war and hatred, and I regret that I did not find a way to avoid mobilisation and my role in the camp. I feel sorry for all the victims, and I curse my own hands for having inflicted pain in any way on innocent people. I wish my sincere words to be understood as a balm for those wounds and as a contribution to the reconciliation of all people in Prijedor and the restoration of the situation that existed before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banovic. You may sit. There being no other business, the hearing is adjourned.
